title: Two Deadlines
teaser: The large shop was cheapest if she signed by the end of September, and the landlord would hold it only until October 16. Yet A-Lan first rented the smaller, more expensive window next door, because what she feared was not one extra month of rent but hard-wiring the wrong shop before she knew what customers would actually return for.
paragraphs: By early September, A-Lan had already finished the layout for her breakfast shop: doors open at six, a large coffee machine on the left, two stacked ovens at the back, and a full breakfast display facing the entrance. The landlord offered two conditions. If she signed for the large unit before the end of September, she would get one month rent-free; after September, the discount disappeared. He would hold the unit for her only until October 16. Signing immediately was actually cheaper in total. The difficult part was that once ventilation, plumbing, wiring, and equipment were installed around this layout, changing it later would be expensive and would require closing the shop again. Her uncertainty was not whether to enter food service. It was when customers would return, and what they would return for.

On September 12, the twelve-square-meter service window next door became available. It was separated from the larger unit by only one door and faced the same pavement and the same mix of office and residential traffic. The landlord would rent it only by the month, at a higher rate per square meter, and the old oven could produce only a limited quantity each day. A-Lan rented it anyway. She stuck a yellow note on the side of the till and wrote “October 16.” If repeat purchases never became stable, she could close the window at month-end. If the data remained mixed, she could rent it for another month. If a pattern became clear, she could still decide whether to take the large unit. She also wrote down the price of keeping those choices open: a temporary sign, moving costs, higher rent, and sales she could not take once the oven sold out.

The first week seemed to prove her original plan right. Opening curiosity created a morning rush, croissants sold out quickly, and coffee and breakfast sets ranked highest in the survey. In the second week, just as many people still passed at seven-thirty, but fewer stopped. The till records began showing a different line instead. After five in the afternoon, some customers from the first week came back, often buying three or four savory breads at once, especially on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Because the window stood beside the future shop, this was not a new customer base from a different neighborhood. What the surveys and pedestrian counts had not captured was who paid a second and a third time.

The weather turned colder in week three, and total sales fell again. A-Lan reopened the large-unit contract for a moment. If overall demand was fading, a handful of evening repeat purchases would not justify expansion. She separated the till data into first-time and repeat customers. Opening-week visitors continued to fall, but most of the evening group had now visited three times. At six on one Thursday, the old oven could not keep up. The final tray of savory bread sold while people were still waiting outside. That night, she spread the original floor plan across the floor and redrew it. The large coffee machine was crossed out, the breakfast display was cut in half, opening time moved from six to ten, and the kitchen was given connections for a second oven—but she did not buy it.

By October 15, the September rent-free offer was definitively gone, and several sellouts at the window had left real sales on the table. The month had not become free simply because it had produced information. After reviewing the four weeks of records, A-Lan signed for the large unit on October 16, but she did not return to the September design. The landlord agreed to split the fit-out into two stages: basic utilities and one main oven first; for the second oven, A-Lan paid only a refundable reservation deposit and kept the decision open until November 30. The window stayed open until month-end, and a buyer had already agreed to take the old oven. If the evening repeat business suddenly disappeared, she could still cancel the second machine.

During the first three weeks in the large unit, morning sales never returned to the level of opening week, while afternoon repeat purchases kept growing. A-Lan did not install the second oven automatically simply because she had already signed the larger lease. She continued recording sellout periods, repeat purchases, and turned-away orders. In the final week of November, demand associated with the second oven had stayed above the minimum level she had set for four consecutive weeks. Only then did she convert the refundable reservation into a firm order. The earlier month in the small window had never proved that “the breakfast shop would succeed.” It had first changed the shape of one irreversible investment, then pushed the next irreversible investment further into the future.

On the evening of November 30, the installer measured the space for the second oven in the back kitchen. A-Lan peeled the yellow note, now curled at the corners, from beside the door. It carried two lines: “October 16” and “November 30.” She crossed out the second date and slipped the note inside the first page of the new oven’s manual.
concept: Real Options emphasizes that when future outcomes are uncertain, major investments are difficult to reverse, and waiting can produce valuable new information, a company can begin with a smaller commitment that can still be stopped. The value lies not only in whatever profit the pilot itself earns, but also in retaining the right to expand, wait, adjust, or exit once new information arrives, and in making major commitments in stages rather than all at once.
explanation: A-Lan does not choose the small window because it is cheaper or more profitable. Its rent rate is higher, and it costs her the rent-free offer and some sales. Its role is to generate real repeat-purchase information from almost the same location while the larger shop’s utilities and equipment are not yet locked into an irreversible design. The first behavioral shift occurs on October 16: she expands after receiving new information, but installs only one main oven. She then postpones the second oven until November 30. The two deadlines break one large commitment into successive decisions that can still be delayed and adjusted.
mapping: Renting the small window at the same location instead of completing the large-unit fit-out → A smaller, terminable commitment is used to obtain transaction data that is closer to the real operating environment.
Repeat purchasing shifts from breakfast toward savory breads in the evening → New information changes the product mix, operating hours, and layout rather than merely confirming the original plan.
Signing the large unit on October 16 but installing only one main oven → After receiving partial information, A-Lan chooses to expand while preserving the option to wait on the next commitment.
Keeping the second oven on a refundable reservation until November 30 → The next irreversible investment is delayed again until additional information is strong enough to support execution.
boundary: A real option has value only when waiting can genuinely produce useful information and the later choices are truly executable. If the pilot environment differs too much from full-scale operations, its information may not be representative. If a location, market opportunity, or price advantage will disappear quickly, the cost of waiting may exceed the value of the information. If contracts cannot be exited, equipment orders cannot be cancelled, or the stages are tightly locked together, the apparent “option” may not be real.
reflection: Between the two deadlines, was A-Lan really buying sales—or buying two chances not to lock in the next step too early?
